# The Tableau companion

Three extracts and a build guide, so the same marts that feed the custom
dashboard can be rebuilt in Tableau in about twenty minutes and the two will
reconcile by construction rather than by coincidence.

**What is here, and what is not.** The three CSV files below are generated by
`make tableau` from the published marts, so they are the same numbers the
dashboard shows. The published workbook is not in this repository, and this
file is honest about why: building a `.twbx` needs Tableau Desktop, and the
machine this project was built on does not have it. The steps below are what
someone with Tableau does next, and the comparison section at the bottom is
written from what each tool can and cannot do rather than from a workbook that
does not exist yet. When the workbook is published, its link goes at the top of
the root README and this paragraph goes away.

## The extracts

| file | grain | rows | what it is for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `zone_month.csv` | month, service, zone | 32,200 | the map and the Pareto |
| `daily.csv` | date, service | 3,840 | the service share over time, with the STL components |
| `hour_of_week.csv` | service, day of week, hour | 504 | the heatmap |

Every column is an additive component, never a rate. That is deliberate and it
matters more in Tableau than anywhere else: a published rate cannot be
re-aggregated, so a `tip_rate` column would be silently wrong the moment
somebody dragged Borough onto the view. Build the rates as calculated fields
over the components, exactly as the metric layer does:

```
Tip rate        SUM([Tip Observable Tip]) / SUM([Tip Observable Fare])
Tipped share    SUM([Tipped Trips]) / SUM([Tip Observable Trips])
Airport share   SUM([Airport Trips]) / SUM([Trips])
Mean duration   SUM([Duration S]) / SUM([Trips]) / 60
Mean speed      SUM([Distance Mi]) / SUM([Duration S]) * 3600
Revenue / mile  SUM([Revenue]) / SUM([Distance Mi])
```

These are the same expressions as the `browser` column of
[`metrics/metrics.yml`](../metrics/metrics.yml), transliterated. If the two ever
differ, the metric layer is right and the workbook is wrong.

## The four sheets

1. **Hour of week heatmap.** `hour_of_week.csv`. Hour on columns, Day Name on
   rows sorted Sunday first, Trips on colour, square marks, the sequential cyan
   ramp below. No borders, a 2px gap between cells.
2. **Zone map.** `zone_month.csv`. Centroid Lon and Centroid Lat as the
   geographic fields, Trips on colour and size, filtered to
   `Has Geometry = true`. Put the excluded share on the title, not in a
   tooltip: unresolved zones carry real volume and a map that silently drops
   them is the failure mode this project is most careful about.
3. **Service share over time.** `daily.csv`. Date on columns, Trips on rows as
   a percent of total table calculation, Service Label on colour, area mark.
   Never a dual axis.
4. **Pareto.** `zone_month.csv`. Zone on columns sorted by Trips descending,
   Trips as a bar, and a running total percent of total as a line, both on one
   axis because both are shares of the same total.

Then one dashboard, laid out for a laptop at 1366 by 768, with the four sheets
and a single filter row for Service, Month and Borough applied to all of them.

## Styling

Turn the default Tableau styling off. It is the single fastest way to make a
workbook look like every other workbook.

- Format, Workbook: set every font to the same family, and set gridlines to
  none on the map and the heatmap, and to a recessive grey elsewhere.
- Delete the automatic titles. Every sheet title should be the question it
  answers, in sentence case, the same way the panels in the custom dashboard
  are headed.
- Colour palette. Add this to `Preferences.tps` in your Tableau repository so
  the assignment is fixed and a filter never repaints a series:

```xml
<?xml version='1.0'?>
<workbook>
  <preferences>
    <color-palette name="cityflow categorical" type="regular">
      <color>#0891B2</color><color>#D97706</color><color>#8B5CF6</color>
      <color>#059669</color><color>#EF4444</color><color>#2563EB</color>
      <color>#EC4899</color><color>#65A30D</color>
    </color-palette>
    <color-palette name="cityflow sequential" type="ordered-sequential">
      <color>#155E75</color><color>#0E7490</color><color>#0891B2</color>
      <color>#06B6D4</color><color>#22D3EE</color><color>#67E8F9</color>
    </color-palette>
    <color-palette name="cityflow diverging" type="ordered-diverging">
      <color>#67E8F9</color><color>#22D3EE</color><color>#0891B2</color>
      <color>#383835</color>
      <color>#D97706</color><color>#B45309</color><color>#92400E</color>
    </color-palette>
  </preferences>
</workbook>
```

Assign the services by hand so they match the custom dashboard: yellow taxi
amber, green taxi emerald, for hire vehicle cyan. These hex values are the
output of `scripts/validate_palette.js`, which checks contrast against the
surface, lightness and chroma separation between adjacent slots, and colour
vision deficiency separation for protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia. They
are not a preference.

## Reconciling the two

After the workbook is built, check it against the warehouse rather than
assuming. The totals in `RESULTS.md` are re-derived by a gate, so they are the
reference:

```bash
uv run cityflow metrics compile tip_rate
```

prints the definition both engines use. If the workbook's tip rate differs from
the figure in `RESULTS.md`, the usual cause is a calculated field written as
`AVG([Tip] / [Fare])` rather than `SUM([Tip]) / SUM([Fare])`, which is the mean
of ratios rather than the ratio of sums and answers a different question.

## What each tool is actually for

Written before the workbook exists, from what the two tools do rather than from
a preference.

**What Tableau gives you in twenty minutes.** The four sheets above, laid out,
filtered and formatted, from three CSV files, with no build step and no
deployment. A map with a working zoom, a heatmap with a working tooltip and a
Pareto with a working running total, none of which had to be written. For
answering "what does the data look like", it is faster than anything else and
it is not close.

**What it cannot do here.** It cannot put a Wilson interval on a rate without a
calculated field per bound written out by hand, and the interval is the point
of the zone ranking panel. It cannot run a multiple comparisons correction at
all, so the panel that states thirty eight comparisons and marks the survivors
has no Tableau equivalent. It cannot show the lineage from a source column to
the number on screen, because it does not know about dbt. And it cannot be
handed to someone as a URL that costs nothing to host: Tableau Public makes the
workbook and its data public, which is fine for this project and is not fine
for most of the work this pattern would be used on.

**Why the custom dashboard exists.** Not because Tableau is insufficient for
charts. Because three of the six panels are about whether the numbers can be
trusted, and those are the panels Tableau has no vocabulary for: intervals on
every rate, a correction for multiple comparisons stated on screen, the
quarantine log, the null rate history, and a lineage graph from source to
pixel. A tool that draws the number well and cannot say where it came from is
the right tool for exploring and the wrong one for publishing.

Both read the same marts. That is the part worth copying.
